newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE-Egypt's child breadwinners toil long hours.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Egypt's child breadwinners toil long hours.

text.p: Face and clothes coated with oil, Ramadan Bayoumi stepped down into the mechanics' pit and probed the innards of the BMW car he was fixing.
"It could be a problem with the gear box," he said, aiming a lamp at the convoluted network of greasy hoses and cylinders.
Bayoumi earns 25 pounds ($7.40) for a 78-hour work week in Harafayeen industrial city outside Cairo. He is 11 years old.
"Yes, it is difficult for the boys, but their families need the salaries," said garage owner Hag Said. "Sometimes Ramadan works well, sometimes so-so. But he's a small boy and he'll get used to it."
About 11 percent of Egypt's workers are children between the ages of 10 to 14, the 15th largest proportion in the world, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) says.
Harafayeen has one of the highest urban concentrations of child labourers in Egypt, with 3,000 children in 1,000 shops, said Harafayeen Development Society Director Taha Shinawi.
The din of buzz saws biting into wood and hammers against steel rang out from the city's one-storey shops and garages.
Herds of sheep skittered along its potholed streets, where boys in soiled work clothes carrying plastic lunch bags passed children with bookbags on their way to school.
Bayoumi and 11-year-old co-worker Ihab Musaad start at Hag Said's garage at nine in the morning and end at 10 at night, breaking for a simple lunch of noodles or cheese.
"Sometimes we work until one in the morning on Saturday, because we have Sunday off," said Musaad.
TWO MILLION WORKING CHILDREN

Official figures say almost 80 percent of child workers are in agriculture, but they overwhelm urban areas as well, weaving through Cairo traffic hawking tissues through car windows, running tea in cafes and operating heavy machinery in workshops.

"I think it's pretty bad here. There mainly is a problem because of the poverty of families," said Georges Salines, a French embassy cooperation centre attache. "Basically everybody agrees on the difficulty of suppressing child labour in Egypt."

The question is how. Activists say moral outrage alone has no currency in a country where at least two million working children below the legal employment age of 15 provide 20 to 30 percent of family income.
"It's not an easy matter. You have to convince families and provide them with alternatives," said ILO official Adel Azer.
The prevalence of child labour in Egypt is also tied to high associated costs of schooling for poor families and the fact that 23 percent of women head households, activists said.
Potential remedies include income generation schemes, Egypt's development funds and micro-credit funds, said UNICEF representative Baquer Namazi in a speech in December.
While not set up wholly for child labour, the Social Fund for Development targets the "ultra-poor", like families with zero to 30 pounds income a month, said SFD consultant Wafiq Hassouna.
Ghada Wali, SFD's community development assistant, said a programme of incentives for workshop owners to release their child workers for health or literacy classes was under study.
Azer said tackling poverty issues was essential. "But if the child has to work, then let him work in a less harmful labour."
ILO WANTS THEM OUT OF WORKSHOPS
That message got lost somewhere in the City of the Dead, where eight-year-old Ramadan Ali works in a pot-making workshop.

Like the 11 other boys up to 14 years of age who toil there, Ramadan looks as if he has been dipped in silver, his face, hands and clothes caked with the burnished residue of the aluminium pots he helps stack in the din and gloom.
Older boys operate heavy lathes, wearing layers of metallic dust like fur around their collars and cobwebs in their hair.
"I earn 10 pounds a week and give it to my family," said Ali, as he paused from scampering around the workshop.

"You've seen the youngest. We didn't want him to work, but it's because of family conditions. He helps support them," said foreman Ahmed Nassar. He said the boys are provided with meals, and a scrub with soap takes care of the silvery coating.

Azer said the ILO wanted to withdraw children under 12 from workshops and from the most dangerous labour, such as working in front of furnaces or in areas where they operate heavy machinery or breathe particles, like in textile or carpet-weaving shops.
And if they cannot be taken out of work, activists say do the next best thing -- try to improve their lives.
SOME PROJECTS PROVIDE RELIEF
"We need an intermediate step for their rights, the right to work reasonable hours, the right to play, to education, and not to be exposed to chemicals, weights and noise," said Salines.
Examples include a UNICEF-supported project in Alexandria serving working children. The government's National Council for Children and Mothers says it also has projects.
The German organisation Friedrich Ebert Stiftung helped start a programme where entrepreneurs pay for teachers at children's workplaces in 10th of Ramadan industrial city.
"It's difficult to convince entrepreneurs. This is not vocational training so there is no direct benefit for them," said project manager Norbert Eder.
But the politics of labour is far from the grassy playground of Al Jeel Centre, where Cairo's working children spend their day off learning to play the lute, read, or throw a frisbee.
Eleven-year-old Karam Hassan, clutching sweets in hands cracked and scaly from his work fixing burners, says he comes for the atmosphere. "I feel human here," he said.
